title: News Feed System
oneLine: Use a hybrid fanout strategy: precompute feeds for normal users, pull celebrity posts at read time, and rank a bounded candidate set.
opening: I would split publishing from feed retrieval. A post is stored once, then an event enters a fanout service. For normal authors, fanout-on-write inserts the post ID into followers’ feed inboxes so reads are fast. For celebrity or extremely high-fanout accounts, I avoid millions of writes and merge their recent posts at read time. The feed service retrieves candidate IDs from a cache, joins post and social metadata, applies privacy blocks and ranking, and returns cursor-based pages. The design is eventually consistent, with idempotent fanout jobs, bounded per-user feed storage, and separate caches for feed IDs, post content, social graph, counters, and actions.
ask: What content types and privacy/block rules apply?
How many followers can one author have?
How fresh must new posts, deletes, and privacy changes appear?
scale: Write amplification = posts/sec × average followers for push fanout; model celebrity tail separately.
Store only a bounded recent feed window per user; older pages can be generated or fetched from durable storage.
Candidate generation and ranking have different latency/cost profiles—cache and degrade them independently.

decisions.default: Hybrid push for normal accounts and pull for celebrities.
decisions.why: Push gives fast reads; pull prevents extreme write amplification.
decisions.switch: Pure pull for small follower graphs or highly dynamic ranking; pure push for bounded enterprise groups.

decisions.default: Generate a bounded candidate set, then rank with features and a timeout.
decisions.why: Ranking every eligible post is too expensive and unpredictable.
decisions.switch: Offer chronological fallback when the ranker is slow or unavailable.

decisions.default: Store ordered post IDs and lightweight scores, not full post copies.
decisions.why: Content updates/deletes remain centralized and memory footprint stays bounded.
decisions.switch: Denormalize immutable snippets at edge for latency, with deletion/version invalidation.

decisions.default: Cursor based on score/time plus stable tie-breaker.
decisions.why: Offset pagination shifts as new posts arrive and becomes expensive at depth.
decisions.switch: Snapshot tokens when a fully stable browsing session is required.

deepDives.title: Celebrity strategy
points: Classify dynamically from follower count and fanout cost.
Pull only recent celebrity posts and merge with inbox candidates.
Cache merged candidates and prevent one celebrity from dominating ranking work.

deepDives.title: Privacy and deletion
points: Filter again at read time even if fanout checked permissions.
Emit delete/privacy-change events to invalidate cached IDs/content.
Use tombstones so old fanout jobs cannot resurrect removed content.

deepDives.title: Ranking degradation
points: Timeout feature calls and use cached/default features.
Keep chronological or lightweight ranking fallback.
Measure freshness, relevance, diversity, and latency separately.

failures.response: Idempotent insert by user+post ID and replayable event log.
Hybrid pull path, rate-controlled fanout, and automatic celebrity threshold.
Read-time authorization, tombstones, cache purge, and event reconciliation.
Bounded timeout and chronological/cached fallback without blocking feed availability.

questions.q: How do you choose the celebrity threshold?
questions.a: From measured fanout cost, queue lag, follower activity, and read frequency—not a fixed follower count alone. Reclassify with hysteresis to avoid thrashing.

questions.q: How do you avoid duplicate posts when merging push and pull?
questions.a: Deduplicate by post ID before ranking and use a stable cursor containing score/time and ID.
Time from post acceptance to eligibility/visibility for active followers, plus delete/privacy propagation latency. Track by author class and region.

questions.q: What if a user follows 100K accounts?
questions.a: Treat it as a whale: cap candidate sources, partition graph reads, use pull-heavy generation, and apply product limits or asynchronous personalized materialization.

mistakes: Storing full post copies in every feed
Using offset pagination on a constantly changing ranked list
seniorSignal: Show that feed generation, candidate retrieval, policy filtering, ranking, hydration, and pagination are separate concerns with independent degradation paths.
implementation: Kafka post/fanout events; worker pools partitioned by author or follower range
Redis sorted sets/lists for bounded feed inboxes
Graph store/cache for follows and blocks
Ranking service with strict deadline and chronological fallback
